title: Problem
body_md: Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions with a critical point at the origin. If there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $\varphi(V(f))=V(g)$, is it true that ${\rm crk}(f)={\rm crk}(g)$?
head: environment
name: Arnold corank problem

title: Theorem
body_md:
{\ref*{thm:corank_mod_two}}
Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions with a critical point at the origin. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $\varphi(V(f))=V(g)$. Then ${\rm crk}(f)\equiv {\rm crk}(g) \mod 2$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
{\ref*{rem:algebraic_corank}}
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero and $f\in k[t][\![ z_1,\dots,z_n ]\! ]$. Write $f_{t}=f(t,\cdot)\in k [\![ z_1,\dots,z_n ]\! ]$; so $t\mapsto f_{t}$ is an algebraic family of formal power series. Assume that the Milnor number of $f_{t}$ is finite, positive, and independent of $t$. Then the corank of $f_t$ is independent of $t$.

title: Conjecture
body_md: Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions. If there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $\varphi(V(f))=V(g)$, then $m(V(f),0)=m(V(g),0)$.
head: environment
name: Zariski multiplicity conjecture

label: conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form}
Let $f,g\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be two holomorphic function-germs. If there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $f=g\circ \varphi$, then $in(f)^{-1}(1)$ and $in(g)^{-1}(1)$ are homotopy equivalent.

title: Notation
body_md: Let $f\colon  (\mathbb{C}^{n}, 0) \to (\mathbb{C}, 0)$ be a holomorphic germ. We denote $V(f)=f^{-1}(0)$ and $F_f$ as the Milnor fiber of $f$ at $0$. When $f$ is a homogeneous polynomial, $F_f=f^{-1}(1)$. Let $m=\text{ord}_0f$ denote the order of $f$ at the origin. Let $in(f)$ denote the initial homogeneous polynomial of degree $m$ in the Taylor expansion of $f$. The multiplicity of $V(f)$ at the origin is denoted by $m(V(f),0)$, which coincides with $\text{ord}_0f$ whenever $f$ is the germ of a reduced function.

title: Theorem
body_md: Let $f,g\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be two complex analytic functions such that there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,V(f),0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,V(g),0)$. If $m(V(f),0)=1$ then $m(V(g),0)=1$ as well.
head: environment
name: A'Campo-L\^e's Theorem

label: thm:acampo_complement
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:acampo_complement}
Let $f\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be a complex analytic function. Then
$$
m(V(f),0)\leq \inf \{k>0;\Lambda(h_f^k)\not=0\}.
$$
Moreover, if $\chi(\mathbb{C} P^{n-1}\setminus PV(in(f)))\not=0$, then
$$
m(V(f),0)=\inf \{k>0;\Lambda(h_f^k)\not=0\}.
$$
head: environment

label: thm:monodromy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:monodromy}
Let $f,g : \mathbb C^{n}\to  \mathbb C$ be two reduced holomorphic  functions. If the germs $(V(f), 0)$ and $(V(g),0)$ are ambient  homeomorphic, then the induced maps in homology of the monodromies of $f$ and $g$ at $0$ are conjugate. In particular, for each positive integer $k$, $\Lambda(h_f^k)=\Lambda(h_g^k)$, and $\chi(F_f ) = \chi(F_g )$.

label: thm:zariski_implies_tangent_conj_Euler_char
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:zariski_implies_tangent_conj_Euler_char}
Let $f,g\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be two reduced holomorphic function-germs. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $f=g\circ \varphi$. If $m(V(f),0)=m(V(g),0)$, then $in(f)^{-1}(1)$ and $in(g)^{-1}(1)$ have the same Euler characteristic.
head: environment

label: prop:formula_euler_charac_monodromy
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\sigma\colon  X_1 \to \mathbb{C}^{n}$ be the blow-up of the origin, and let $E_0 \cong \mathbb{C}P^{n-1}$ be the resulting exceptional divisor.
Let $\pi: X \to \mathbb{C}^{n}$ be a resolution of singularities extending the blow-up of the origin and where the total transform divisor $D = \pi^{-1}(V(f))$ has normal crossings. The stratum $S_k$ is the set of points $x \in \pi^{-1}(0)$ where the local equation of $D$ is a pure power of the form $z^k = 0$. 
This definition excludes points where the divisor has normal crossings (e.g., $z_1^a z_2^b = 0$). Thus, $S_k$ is locally closed and contains no intersection points of components of the divisor. It is easy to obtain the following:


    
\begin{claim}\label{claim:complement_proj_tg_cone}
For $m = m(V(f), 0)$, the stratum $S_m$ is diffeomorphic to the complement of the projectivized tangent cone:
\[ S_m \cong \mathbb{C}P^{n-1} \setminus PV(in(f)). \]
Furthermore, $S_k = \emptyset$ for all $k < m$.
\end{claim}
\begin{comment}

                                                                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                             

                                                                                                    
                                             

                                                  
                 
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
               

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
                                                                                                    

                                                                                             
                                                                                                 
           
\end{comment}

We use the trace formula for the Lefschetz number established in \cite[Theorem 1]{ACampo:1975}:
\[ \Lambda(h_f^k) = \sum_{d | k} d \cdot \chi(S_d). \]
We evaluate this for $k=m$. By Claim \ref{claim:complement_proj_tg_cone}, $S_d = \emptyset$ for all $d < m$. Therefore, the sum reduces to the single term $d=m$:
\begin{equation} \label{eq:trace}
    \Lambda(h_f^m) = m \cdot \chi(S_m).
\end{equation}
From Claim \ref{claim:complement_proj_tg_cone}, we have
\begin{equation} \label{eq:geom_subs}
    \Lambda(h_f^m) = m \cdot \chi(\mathbb{C}P^{n-1} \setminus PV(in(f))).
\end{equation}

Now, consider the Milnor fiber of the homogeneous polynomial $in(f)$:
\[ F_{in(f)} = \{ z \in \mathbb{C}^{n} \mid in(f)(z) = 1 \}. \]
Define the projection $\rho\colon F_{in(f)} \to \mathbb{C}P^{n-1} \setminus PV(in(f))$ by $\rho(z) = [z]$.
For any $[z_0] \in \mathbb{C}P^{n-1} \setminus PV(in(f))$, we have $in(f)(z_0) \neq 0$. The points in the fiber $\rho^{-1}([z_0])$ are vectors $\lambda z_0$ satisfying:
\[ in(f)(\lambda z_0) = \lambda^m \cdot in(f)(z_0) = 1 \implies \lambda^m = \frac{1}{in(f)(z_0)}. \]
This equation has exactly $m$ distinct roots for $\lambda$. Thus, $\rho$ is an unramified covering map of degree $m$.
The Euler characteristic of the total space of a finite covering is the degree times the Euler characteristic of the base:
\[ \chi(F_{in(f)}) = m \cdot \chi(\mathbb{C}P^{n-1} \setminus PV(in(f))). \]
Comparing this with equation (\ref{eq:geom_subs}), we obtain the desired result:
\[ \Lambda(h_f^m) = \chi(F_{in(f)}). \]

label: thm:zariski_equiv_tangent_conj_Euler_char
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:zariski_equiv_tangent_conj_Euler_char}
Conjecture \ref{conj:zariski_right} has a positive answer if and only if Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_Euler_char} has a positive answer.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem \ref{thm:zariski_implies_tangent_conj_Euler_char}, we only need to prove that if Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_Euler_char} has a positive answer, then Conjecture \ref{conj:zariski_right} also has a positive answer.

So, assume that Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_Euler_char} has a positive answer. 

Let $f,g\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be two reduced holomorphic function-germs. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $f=g\circ \varphi$. We have to prove that $m(V(f),0)=m(V(g),0)$. 

Since Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_Euler_char} has a positive answer, $\chi(F_{in(f)})=\chi(F_{in(g)})$. We have two cases to consider.

\noindent $\bullet$ {\bf Case $\chi(F_{in(f)})=\chi(F_{in(g)})\not =0$.} 

This implies $\chi(\mathbb{C} P^{n-1}\setminus PV(in(f)))\not=0$ and  $\chi(\mathbb{C} P^{n-1}\setminus PV(in(g)))\not=0$. By Theorem \ref{thm:acampo_complement},
$$
m(V(f),0)=\inf \{j>0;\Lambda(h_f^j)\not=0\}
$$
and 
$$
m(V(g),0)=\inf \{j>0;\Lambda(h_g^j)\not=0\}.
$$
By Theorem \ref{thm:monodromy}, $\Lambda(h_g^j)=\Lambda(h_f^j)$ for all positive integers $j$. Therefore, $m(V(f),0)=m(V(g),0)$.

\noindent $\bullet$ {\bf Case $\chi(F_{in(f)})=\chi(F_{in(g)})=0$.} 

For simplicity, let $m=m(V(f),0)$ and $k=m(V(g),0)$.
Assume by contradiction that $m\not= k$. We may assume that $m<k$. Since $m\geq 2$, we have that $k\geq 3$. 

Let us define $\tilde f, \tilde g\colon (\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{C},0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ by
$\tilde f(x,t)=f(x)+t^k$ and $\tilde g(x,t)=g(x)+t^k$. Then, the homeomorphism $\tilde\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n\times \mathbb{C},0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n\times \mathbb{C},0)$ given by $\tilde \varphi(x,t)=(\varphi(x),t)$ satisfies $\tilde f=\tilde g\circ \tilde \varphi$. 
Since we are assuming that Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_Euler_char} has a positive answer, we have $\chi(F_{in(\tilde f)})=\chi(F_{in(\tilde g)})$. However, $in(\tilde f)(x,t)=in(f)(x)$ and  $in(\tilde g)(x,t)=in(g)(x)+t^k$. Then, $F_{in(\tilde f)}=F_{in(f)}\times \mathbb{C}$, and $F_{in(\tilde g)}$ is homotopy equivalent to the join of $F_{in(g)}$ and $F_k:=\{t\in \mathbb{C}; t^k=1\}$, denoted here by $F_{in(g)}\ast F_k$. Then, $\chi(F_{in(\tilde f)})=\chi(F_{in(f)})=0$. 

To calculate $\chi(F_{in(\tilde g)})$ we need the following result, which may be well-known, but we were unable to find a proper reference for it. Thus, we decided to present a proof of it.
\begin{lemma}
For any finite CW-complexes $X$ and $Y$, the Euler characteristic of their join satisfies:
\[
\chi(X * Y) =1-(\chi(X)-1)(\chi(Y)-1).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}

It is a standard result that the join $X * Y$ is homotopy equivalent to the suspension of the smash product:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relation_join-smash-suspension}
    X * Y \simeq \Sigma(X \wedge Y),
\end{equation}
where $X \wedge Y$ denotes the smash product and $\Sigma(Z)$ denotes the unreduced suspension of the topological space $Z$.
Recall that by definition, the smash product is the quotient space $X \wedge Y = (X \times Y) / (X \vee Y)$, where $X \vee Y$ denotes the wedge of $X$ and $Y$.

For finite CW-complexes, the Euler characteristic of a quotient pair $(A, B)$ satisfies $\chi(A/B) = \chi(A) - \chi(B) + 1$. Applying this property, we obtain:
\[
\chi(X \wedge Y) = \chi(X \times Y) - \chi(X \vee Y) + 1.
\]
Using that $\chi(X \times Y) = \chi(X)\chi(Y)$ and the additive property for wedge sums $\chi(X \vee Y) = \chi(X) + \chi(Y) - 1$, we substitute to find:
\begin{align*}
\chi(X \wedge Y) &= \chi(X)\chi(Y) - \big(\chi(X) + \chi(Y) - 1\big) + 1 \\
&= \chi(X)\chi(Y) - \chi(X) - \chi(Y) + 2.
\end{align*}
Therefore,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smash_prod_formula}
\chi(X \wedge Y) = 1+(\chi(X)-1)(\chi(Y)-1).    
\end{equation}


Taking the unreduced suspension of a space shifts its reduced homology groups up by exactly one degree, meaning $\tilde{H}_{k}(\Sigma (Z)) \cong \tilde{H}_{k-1}(Z)$ for all $k$. Because the Euler characteristic is the alternating sum of the ranks of these homology groups, shifting the degrees by one flips the sign of the entire sum. Thus, for any space $Z$:
\[
\chi(\Sigma (Z)) -1= 1-\chi(Z).
\]
Combining this sign reversal with the homotopy equivalence $X * Y \simeq \Sigma(X \wedge Y)$ and Equation (\ref{eq:smash_prod_formula}), we conclude:
\begin{align*}
\chi(X * Y)-1 & = \chi\big(\Sigma(X \wedge Y)\big) -1\\
              & = 1 -\chi(X \wedge Y) \\
              & = 1-(1+(\chi(X)-1)(\chi(Y)-1))
\end{align*}
Therefore
\[
\chi(X * Y) =1-(\chi(X)-1)(\chi(Y)-1).
\]
\end{proof}
Then, 
$$
0=\chi(F_{in(\tilde f)})=\chi(F_{in(\tilde g)})=1-(\chi(F_{in(g)})-1)(\chi(F_k)-1)=\chi(F_k)=k\not =0,
$$
which is a contradiction. 

Therefore, we must have $m=k$.

label: prop:semi_top_mult
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:semi_top_mult}
Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be two reduced holomorphic functions. Assume that $f$ and $g$ are generalized semi-Brieskorn-Pham functions and that there is a homeomorphism $\phi\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $\phi(V(f))=V(g)$. If $m(V(f),0),m(V(g),0)\not=2$, then $m(V(f),0)=m(V(g),0)$ and $m_1(f)=m_1(g)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
After a change of coordinates, if necessary, we may assume that $f$ and $g$ are written in the following way:
$$
f(z_1,...,z_r,z_{r+1},...,z_n)=z_1^{a}+...+z_r^{a}+h(z_{1},...,z_n),
$$
and 
$$
g(z_1,...,z_s,z_{s+1},...,z_n)=z_1^{b}+...+z_s^{b}+\tilde h(z_{1},...,z_n),
$$
where $h,\tilde h\colon (\mathbb{C}^{n},0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ are holomorphic functions such that ${\rm ord}_0 h>a$ and ${\rm ord}_0 \tilde h>b$. In this case, $in(f)(z)= z_1^{a}+...+z_r^{a}$ and $in(g)(z)= z_1^{b}+...+z_s^{b}$, where $r=m_1(f)$ and $r=m_1(g)$. 

Note that if $r>1$, then $\chi(F_{in(f)})=1+(-1)^{r-1}(a-1)^r$, and if $r=1$, then $\chi(F_{in(f)})=a>0$. By the same reasoning, if $s>1$, then $\chi(F_{in(g)})=1+(-1)^{s-1}(b-1)^s$, and if $s=1$, then $\chi(F_{in(g)})=b>0$.

From Proposition \ref{prop:formula_euler_charac_monodromy}, $\Lambda(h_f^a)=\chi(F_{in(f)})$ and $\Lambda(h_g^b)=\chi(F_{in(g)})$. 
Since $a,b>2$, we have that $\Lambda(h_f^a)\not=0$ and $\Lambda(h_g^b)\not =0$. Therefore, by Theorem \ref{thm:acampo_complement}, $a=b$, and $\chi(F_{in(f)})=\chi(F_{in(g)})$. Thus, if $r,s>1$, then 
$$
1+(-1)^{r-1}(a-1)^r=1+(-1)^{s-1}(a-1)^s,
$$
which forces $r=s$.

Since $a>2$, $m=1$ is the unique integer solution for the following equation
$$
a=1+(-1)^{m-1}(a-1)^m.
$$
Thus, $r=1$ if and only if $s=1$.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be two reduced holomorphic functions such that $C(V(f),0)$ is a linear subspace. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\phi\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $\phi(V(f))=V(g)$. Then $m(V(f),0)\geq m(V(g),0)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $C(V(f),0)$ is a linear subspace, $m_1(f)=1$. Thus, after a change of coordinates, if necessary, we may assume that $f$ is written in the following way:
$$
f(z_1,...,z_n)=z_1^{a}+h(z_{1},...,z_n),
$$
where $h\colon (\mathbb{C}^{n},0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ is a holomorphic function such that ${\rm ord}_0 h>a$. In this case, $in(f)(z)= z_1^{a}$ and $\chi(F_{in(f)})=a>0$.

From Proposition \ref{prop:formula_euler_charac_monodromy}, $\Lambda(h_f^a)=\chi(F_{in(f)})$. Thus, $\Lambda(h_g^a)=\Lambda(h_f^a)=a\not=0$. Therefore, by Theorem \ref{thm:acampo_complement}, $a=m(V(f),0)\geq m(V(g),0)$.

title: Corollary

title: Corollary
body_md: Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be two reduced holomorphic functions such that $C(V(f),0)$ and $C(V(g),0)$ are linear subspaces. Let $a_1,...,a_r,b_1,...,b_r\geq 3$ be integers, and $\tilde f,\tilde g\colon (\mathbb{C}^{n+r},0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be the functions $\tilde f(x_1,...,x_{n+1})=x_1^{a_1}+...+x_r^{a_r}+f(x_{r+1},...,x_{n+r})$ and $\tilde g(x_1,...,x_{n+r})=x_1^{b_1}+...+x_r^{b_r}+g(x_{r+1},...,x_{n+1})$. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\phi\colon (\mathbb{C}^{n+1},0)\to (\mathbb{C}^{n+1},0)$ such that $\phi(V(\tilde f))=V(\tilde g)$. Then $m(V(\tilde f),0)=m(V(\tilde g),0)$.

label: thm:corank_mod_two
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:corank_mod_two}
Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions with a critical point at the origin. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ such that $\varphi(V(f))=V(g)$. Then ${\rm crk}(f)\equiv {\rm crk}(g) \mod 2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Instead of proving ${\rm crk}(f)\equiv {\rm crk}(g) \mod 2$, we are going to prove ${\rm rk}(f)\equiv {\rm rk}(g) \mod 2$.

Firstly, assume that ${\rm rk}(f)\equiv 1 \mod 2$. Then, after a holomorphic change of coordinates, we may assume that
$$
f(z_1,...,z_n)=z_1^2+...+z_{2k+1}^2+h(z_{1},...,z_n),
$$
where $h$ is holomorphic with ${\rm ord}_0h>2$. By Proposition \ref{prop:formula_euler_charac_monodromy},
\[ \Lambda(h_f^2) = \chi(F_{in(f)})=1+(-1)^{2k}=2\not=0. \]
By Theorem \ref{thm:acampo_complement}, $\Lambda(h_g^2)\not= 0$ and $m(V(g),0)\leq 2$. By A'Campo-L\^e's Theorem, $m(V(g),0)=2$. Then, after a holomorphic change of coordinates, we may assume that
$$
g(z_1,...,z_n)=z_1^2+...+z_{s}^2+\tilde h(z_{1},...,z_n),
$$
where $s={\rm rk}(f)$, and $\tilde h$ is holomorphic with ${\rm ord}_0\tilde h>2$. By Proposition \ref{prop:formula_euler_charac_monodromy},
\[ \Lambda(h_g^2) = \chi(F_{in(g)})=1+(-1)^{s-1}. \]
Since $\Lambda(h_g^2) =\Lambda(h_f^2) =2$, then $s$ is an odd number and thus ${\rm rk}(f)\equiv {\rm rk}(g) \mod 2$.

Now, assume that ${\rm rk}(f)\equiv 0 \mod 2$. Then, the first part of this proof forces ${\rm rk}(g)\equiv 0 \mod 2$. Then, ${\rm rk}(f)\equiv {\rm rk}(g) \mod 2$.

Therefore, in any case, ${\rm rk}(f)\equiv {\rm rk}(g) \mod 2$, and thus ${\rm crk}(f)\equiv {\rm crk}(g) \mod 2$.

label: cor:corank_dim_two
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:corank_dim_two}
Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^2,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions with a critical point at the origin. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^2,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^2,0)$ such that $\varphi(V(f))=V(g)$. Then ${\rm crk}(f)= {\rm crk}(g)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $r={\rm rk}(f)$ and $s={\rm rk}(g)$.

Since the multiplicity is an embedded topological invariant in $\mathbb{C}^2$, we have that ${\rm rk}(f)\not= 0$ if and only if ${\rm rk}(g)\not =0$. Thus, we may assume that $r,s\geq 1$, which implies $r,s\in \{1,2\}$.

By Theorem \ref{thm:corank_mod_two}, ${\rm crk}(f)\equiv {\rm crk}(g) \mod 2$. Then $r\equiv s \mod 2$. Since $r,s\in \{1,2\}$, we have $r=s$.

label: thm:corank_dim_three
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:corank_dim_three}
Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^3,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions with a critical point at the origin. Assume that there is a homeomorphism $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^3,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^3,0)$ such that $\varphi(V(f))=V(g)$. Then ${\rm crk}(f)= {\rm crk}(g)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since ${\rm crk}(f)=3-{\rm rk}(f)$ and ${\rm crk}(g) =3-{\rm rk}(g)$, it is enough to prove that ${\rm rk}(f)={\rm rk}(f)$. Let $r={\rm rk}(f)$ and $s={\rm rk}(g)$.

Since the multiplicity equal to 2 is an embedded topological invariant in $\mathbb{C}^3$ (see \cite{Aznar:1980} or \cite{FernandesJS:2025}), we have that ${\rm rk}(f)\not= 0$ if and only if ${\rm rk}(g)\not =0$. Thus, we may assume that $r,s\geq 1$. 

Suppose that $r=3$. Then, after a change of coordinates, if necessary, we may assume that $in(f)(z_1,z_2,z_3)= z_1^2+z_2^2+z_3^2$. Then $f$ has an isolated singularity at $0$, and $\mu(f)=1$. Then, $g$ also has an isolated singularity at $0$ and $\mu(g)=1$. Therefore, $s=3$ as well.

Thus, we may assume that $r,s\in \{1,2\}$.
By Theorem \ref{thm:corank_mod_two}, ${\rm crk}(f)\equiv {\rm crk}(g) \mod 2$. Then $r\equiv s \mod 2$. Therefore, if $r=1$ then $s=1$, and if $r=2$ then $s=2$.

Therefore, in any case, $r=s$.

title: Theorem
body_md: If Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_homology} has a positive answer, then the Arnold corank problem for right topological equivalence also has a positive answer.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f,g\colon (\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C},0)$ be germs of reduced holomorphic functions with a critical point at the origin, and $\varphi\colon(\mathbb{C}^n,0)\to (\mathbb{C}^n,0)$ be a homeomorphism such that $f=g\circ \varphi$.

Assume that Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_homology} has a positive answer. By \cite{Sampaio:2026}, $m(V(f),0)=m(V(g),0)$.
We may assume that $m(V(f),0)=m(V(g),0)=2$.
Let $r={\rm rk}(f)$ and $s={\rm rk}(g)$. Thus, $r,s\geq 1$.
Then $\widetilde{H}_{r-1}(in(f)^{-1}(1))=\mathbb{Z}$, $\widetilde{H}_{j}(in(f)^{-1}(1))=0$ for $j\not\in\{0,r-1\}$, and
$$
\widetilde{H}_0(in(f)^{-1}(1))=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\mathbb{Z},     & \mbox{if } r=1 \\
0,     &  \mbox{if } r>1.
\end{array}\right.
$$
Similarly, $\widetilde{H}_{s-1}(in(g)^{-1}(1))=\mathbb{Z}$, $\widetilde{H}_{j}(in(g)^{-1}(1))=0$ for $j\not\in\{0,s-1\}$, and 
$$
\widetilde{H}_0(in(g)^{-1}(1))=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\mathbb{Z},     & \mbox{if } s=1 \\
0,     &  \mbox{if } s>1.
\end{array}\right.
$$
Since Conjecture \ref{conj:Milnor_fiber_initial_form_homology} has a positive answer, we have 
$$
\widetilde{H}_j(in(f)^{-1}(1))\cong \widetilde{H}_j(in(g)^{-1}(1))\text{ for all }j. 
$$
Then $r=s$ and therefore ${\rm crk}(f)={\rm crk}(g).$

label: thm:corank_family
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:corank_family}
Let $\{f_t\}_t$ be a continuous family of holomorphic functions. If the Milnor number $\mu(f_t)$ is independent of $t$, finite, and positive, then the corank ${\rm crk}(f_t)$ is also independent of $t$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $t$, let $F_{t}=\{x\in \mathbb{C}^n;in(f_t)(x)=1\}$.
Let $r_t={\rm rk}(f_t)$. By \cite[Thereom 1.1]{BobadillaP:2022}, we may assume $r_t,r_0\geq 1$.

Then $\widetilde{H}^{r_t-1}(F_t)=\mathbb{Z}$, $\widetilde{H}^{j}(F_t)=0$ for $j\not\in\{0,r_t-1\}$, and
$$
\widetilde{H}^0(F_t)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\mathbb{Z},     & \mbox{if } r_t=1 \\
0,     &  \mbox{if } r_t>1.
\end{array}\right.
$$
By \cite[Remark 8.2]{BobadillaP:2022}, $H_*^{BM}(F_t)=H_*^{BM}(F_0)$, where $H_*^{BM}(F)$ denotes the Borel-Moore homology of $F$. Since each $F_t$ is an oriented smooth manifold of real dimension $2n-2$, Poincaré duality gives an isomorphism modulo torsion between Borel-Moore homology and singular cohomology:
$$
H_*^{BM}(F_t)=H^{2n-2-*}(F_t).
$$
So, $H^{*}(F_t)=H^{*}(F_0)$, and then $r_t=r_0$. Therefore, ${\rm crk}(f_t)={\rm crk}(f_0).$

label: cor:corank_non-isolated_one
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Applying inductively the uniform L\^e--Iomdine formulas \cite[Theorem 4.5]{Massey:1995}, we have that for some $j>2$, $k\in \{0,\dots, n\}$, and $a_1,\dots,a_k\in \mathbb{C}\setminus \{0\}$, the singularity $g_t=f_{t}+a_1z_1^{j}+\dots+a_kz_{k}^{j}$ is isolated, and its sequence of L\^e numbers, which in this case consists solely of the Milnor number $\mu(g_t)$ (see \cite[Example 2.1]{Massey:1995}), is independent of $t$.
    
 By Theorem \ref{thm:corank_family}, the corank of $g_t$ is independent of $t$. Since $j>2$, we have that ${\rm crk}(f_t)={\rm crk}(g_t)$; thus, the corank of $f_t$ is independent of $t$.
head: environment

label: cor:corank_non-isolated_two
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By \cite[Corollary 7.8]{Massey:1995}, for any coordinate system on $\mathbb{C}^n$, all L\^e numbers of $f_t$ are independent of $t$. By Corollary \ref{cor:corank_non-isolated_one}, the corank of $f_t$ is independent of $t$.

label: rem:algebraic_corank
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{rem:algebraic_corank}
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero and $f\in k[t][\![ z_1,\dots,z_n ]\! ]$. Write $f_{t}=f(t,\cdot)\in k [\![ z_1,\dots,z_n ]\! ]$; so $t\mapsto f_{t}$ is an algebraic family of formal power series. Assume that the Milnor number of $f_{t}$ is finite, positive, and independent of $t$. Then the corank of $f_t$ is independent of $t$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $t$, the formal power series $f_t$ has a finite Milnor number $\mu$, implying it is finitely determined. Because the Milnor number is assumed to be independent of $t$, the degree of determinacy is uniformly bounded across the entire family. So, we can replace the formal power series $f$ by its polynomial truncation $f^{(N)} = \sum_{|I|<N} a_{I} z^{I}$ for some integer $N$ (for instance, $N = \mu + 2$) that is independent of $t$. Here, the coefficients $a_{I}$ belong to $k[t]$. This truncation is right-equivalent to the original series $f_t$; consequently, it preserves the Milnor number and the corank (which is completely determined by the $2$-jet of $f_t$).

The truncated family is defined by a finite collection of polynomials $a_I(t) \in k[t]$. Let $S \subset k$ be the finite set consisting of all coefficients of these polynomials $a_I$. We define $k_{0} = \mathbb{Q}(S)$ as the field extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ generated by the elements of $S$. Since $k_{0}$ is a finitely generated field extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, we have an embedding $k_{0}\hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. 

Now, the algebraic family $\{f_{t}\}_t$ can be treated as a family in $\mathbb{C}[t][z_1,\dots,z_n]$. Under this identification, $\{f_{t}\}_t$ constitutes a $\mu$-constant family of isolated complex hypersurface singularities. By Theorem \ref{thm:corank_family}, the corank of $f_{t}$ does not depend on $t$.
